items.title: Physics I — Units, Motion, Force, Gravitation & Fluids
items.body:
### Units, motion and force

**In one line**
This is the grammar of physics: the units we measure in, how we describe moving bodies, and the three Newton rules that say why they move.

**The story**
Every measurement needs an agreed yardstick. Scientists agreed on **seven base units** — everything else (force, energy, power) is built from them, so these are called *derived* units. Once you can measure length and time you can describe **motion**: how fast (speed), how fast and in which direction (velocity), and how quickly the velocity changes (acceleration). Newton then explained *why* motion changes: a body keeps doing what it is doing unless a force acts (first law), a force changes its motion in proportion to the force and inversely to its mass (second law, F = ma), and every push produces an equal push back (third law).

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
APPSC repeatedly asks SI base-vs-derived units, scalar-vs-vector sorting, and one-line statements of Newton's laws. These are single-fact or multi-statement items that are easy marks if the definitions are crisp.

**Picture it**

| Topic | Key facts |
|---|---|
| Seven base units | metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (current), kelvin (temperature), mole (amount), candela (luminous intensity) |
| Derived units | newton (force), joule (energy), watt (power), pascal (pressure), hertz (frequency) |
| Scalars (size only) | distance, speed, mass, energy |
| Vectors (size + direction) | displacement, velocity, acceleration, force |
| Newton's laws | 1 = inertia · 2 = F = ma · 3 = equal and opposite forces on two different bodies |

**Terms explained**
- **Scalar** — a quantity with size only (speed = 60 km/h).
- **Vector** — a quantity with size and direction (velocity = 60 km/h north).
- **Inertia** — the tendency of a body to resist a change in its state of rest or motion.
- **Momentum** — mass multiplied by velocity; it is conserved (stays the same total) in collisions.
- **g** — acceleration due to gravity, about 9.8 metres per second each second near Earth's surface.

**Reading a graph of motion** — on a velocity–time graph, the **slope** (steepness) is the acceleration and the **area under the line is the displacement**. Acceleration itself is simply the rate of change of velocity (change in velocity ÷ time).

**Equations of motion** (straight line, constant acceleration): v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as, where u = starting speed, v = final speed, a = acceleration, t = time, s = distance.

### Gravitation and fluids

**The story (continued)**
Gravity pulls every mass towards every other mass (Newton's universal law, F = G·m₁m₂ divided by r²). Near Earth this gives the value **g**. Because Earth is slightly flattened, you are a little closer to the centre at the poles, so g is a touch larger there (about 9.83) than at the equator (about 9.78). Your **mass** never changes, but your **weight** (W = mg) does, because it depends on g — on the Moon g is only one-sixth, so you weigh one-sixth as much. At the very centre of the Earth g becomes zero, so a body's weight there is zero. **g does not depend on the mass of the falling body** — ignoring air, a heavy stone and a light stone dropped together land together (Galileo). In liquids and gases, Archimedes saw that a submerged body is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of fluid it shoves aside; if that upward push (the **buoyant force**) can balance the body's weight, the body floats — so a body floats when its weight is less than or equal to the maximum buoyant force available when it is fully submerged. A **hydrometer** (which measures the density of liquids such as milk) works on this principle of flotation: it sinks deeper in a lighter liquid. Air also presses on us: atmospheric pressure decreases with increasing altitude, because there is less air above.

**Picture it**

| Idea | Rule |
|---|---|
| Value of g | greater at poles (~9.83) than equator (~9.78); one-sixth on the Moon; zero at Earth's centre |
| Weight vs mass | mass constant everywhere; weight W = mg varies with g |
| Pressure in a fluid | P = hρg — rises with depth; atmospheric pressure ≈ 101 kilopascals at sea level, falls with altitude |
| Archimedes' principle | upthrust = weight of fluid displaced; a body floats when its average density is less than the fluid's |
| Work and power | Work = force × distance × cosθ (zero when force is at right angles to movement); Power = work ÷ time, SI unit the watt (the joule is the unit of work/energy, not power); 1 horsepower ≈ 746 watts |
| Energy | kinetic energy (energy of motion) = ½mv²; potential energy (energy of height) = mgh; energy is conserved — it only changes form |

**Don't confuse**
- **Mass vs weight** — mass is the amount of matter (kilograms, constant); weight is the gravitational pull on it (newtons, changes with g).
- **Speed vs velocity** — speed has no direction; velocity does, so a body in a circle at steady speed still has changing velocity.
- **Third law bodies** — action and reaction are equal and opposite but act on *two different* bodies, so they never cancel out.

**Remember it**
Newton in order is "**1-2-3 = Inertia, F = ma, Pairs**"; and "a ship floats because it pushes aside more water-weight than it weighs".

**TL;DR**
- Seven SI base units; newton/joule/watt/pascal are derived.
- Displacement, velocity, acceleration, force are vectors; distance, speed, mass are scalars.
- Newton: inertia → F = ma → equal-opposite pairs on different bodies; momentum = mass × velocity.
- g is bigger at the poles and one-sixth on the Moon; weight changes with g, mass does not.
- Archimedes: upthrust = weight of displaced fluid; float when density < fluid's; 1 HP ≈ 746 W.
keyPoints: Seven SI base units include kelvin (temperature) and mole (amount); newton/joule/watt are derived.
Displacement, velocity and acceleration are vectors; distance and speed are scalars.
Newton's 1st law = inertia; 2nd law F = ma; 3rd law action-reaction act on different bodies.
Momentum = mass × velocity and is conserved in collisions.
g is greater at the poles than the equator and about one-sixth on the Moon; weight = mg, mass is constant.
Work = force × distance × cosθ (zero when force is perpendicular to displacement); 1 horsepower ≈ 746 watts.
Archimedes' principle: upthrust = weight of displaced fluid; a body floats if its density < fluid's; pressure P = hρg.
Frequency link: humans hear 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; infrasound is below 20 Hz and ultrasound is above 20,000 Hz (details in Light, sound and heat).

items.title: Physics II — Light, Sound & Heat
items.body:
### Light — mirrors, lenses and colour

**In one line**
Light bounces off surfaces (reflection) and bends when it changes medium (refraction), and these two behaviours explain mirrors, spectacles and the rainbow.

**The story**
When light hits a smooth surface it bounces off at the same angle it arrived — the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. A **concave** mirror curves inward and brings rays together (converging), so it is used in torches, headlights and shaving mirrors; a **convex** mirror curves outward and spreads rays (diverging), giving an erect (upright), diminished (smaller) image and a wide view, which is why it is the vehicle rear-view mirror. When light passes from air into glass or water it bends — this is refraction. A **convex lens** is fat in the middle and converges light (a magnifying glass; corrects long sight); a **concave lens** is thin in the middle and diverges light (corrects short sight). A glass prism bends the colours of white light by different amounts, splitting it into the familiar sequence **VIBGYOR** (violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red) — this spreading is called dispersion, and the rainbow is dispersion plus reflection inside raindrops.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
Mirror and lens type (converging vs diverging), the rear-view-mirror example, eye-defect corrections and the word 'dispersion' are classic single-fact and statement MCQs.

**Picture it**

| Device | Behaviour | Everyday use |
|---|---|---|
| Concave mirror | converges | headlights, shaving mirror |
| Convex mirror | diverges | rear-view mirror (wide view) |
| Convex lens | converges | magnifying glass; corrects hypermetropia (long sight) |
| Concave lens | diverges | corrects myopia (short sight) |

### Sound and heat

**The story (continued)**
Sound is a **mechanical wave** — it needs particles to travel, so it cannot cross a vacuum, and it moves fastest where particles are packed tightest: solids beat liquids beat gases (about 343 metres per second in air). Humans hear 20 to 20,000 vibrations per second; below that is infrasound, above it is ultrasound. SONAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging) uses ultrasonic waves: it sends ultrasound into the sea and times the echo to measure depth. **Heat** moves in three ways: conduction through touching solids, convection by moving fluids (sea and land breezes), and radiation which needs no medium at all — that is how the Sun's heat crosses empty space. Water takes in a lot of heat for a small temperature rise (high specific heat), so it keeps coastal climates mild; **latent heat** is the heat a substance swallows to change state (ice to water) without its temperature rising.

**Picture it**

| Mode | Needs a medium? | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Conduction | yes (solids) | heating a metal rod |
| Convection | yes (fluids) | sea breeze, boiling water |
| Radiation | no (works in vacuum) | heat from the Sun |

**Terms explained**
- **Converging** — rays brought together to a point.
- **Diverging** — rays spread apart.
- **Dispersion** — splitting of white light into its colours (red to violet).
- **Ultrasound** — sound above 20,000 vibrations per second, too high for humans to hear.
- **Latent heat** — heat taken in or given out during a change of state, at constant temperature.

**Don't confuse**
- **Concave vs convex** — a concave mirror converges but a convex *lens* converges; the names behave oppositely for mirrors and lenses.
- **Ultrasound vs infrasound** — ultrasound is *above* 20,000 Hz (SONAR); infrasound is *below* 20 Hz.
- **Latent vs specific heat** — latent heat changes state at fixed temperature; specific heat changes temperature.

**Remember it**
"Radiation is the only heat that travels through nothing — that is why we feel the Sun."

**TL;DR**
- Concave mirror and convex lens converge; convex mirror and concave lens diverge; rear-view = convex mirror.
- A prism disperses white light into red-to-violet; refraction is light bending between media.
- Sound needs a medium, is fastest in solids; audible range 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; ultrasound (>20,000 Hz) drives SONAR.
- Heat: conduction (solids), convection (fluids), radiation (works in vacuum).
- Water's high specific heat moderates coastal climate; latent heat changes state at constant temperature.
keyPoints: Concave mirror converges (headlights, shaving); convex mirror diverges (rear-view, wide view).
Convex lens is converging and corrects hypermetropia; concave lens is diverging and corrects myopia.
A prism disperses white light into red-to-violet; refraction is the bending of light between media.
Sound needs a medium (no sound in vacuum) and travels fastest in solids; audible range 20 Hz-20 kHz.
Ultrasound (>20 kHz) is used in SONAR to measure sea depth; echo is reflected sound.
Heat transfer: conduction (solids), convection (fluids), radiation (works in vacuum, e.g. the Sun).

items.title: Physics III — Electricity, Magnetism & Modern Physics
items.body:
### Electricity and magnetism

**In one line**
Electric current is the flow of charge through a circuit, and a changing magnet can create that current — the link that powers generators and motors.

**The story**
In a circuit, voltage pushes current through resistance, and Ohm found these are proportional: V = IR — **Ohm's law holds at constant temperature** (a hot wire's resistance changes). Join components one after another (**series**) and the same current flows through each; join them side by side (**parallel**) and each gets the full voltage, which is how house wiring works so one switch does not kill the rest. A **fuse** is a thin wire placed *in series* in the live line; if too much current flows it heats up and melts, breaking the circuit before a fire starts. Oersted noticed a current makes a magnetic field, and Faraday found the reverse — moving a magnet near a coil *induces* a current; this is the principle of **electromagnetic induction**. This two-way link is the heart of technology: a **generator** turns motion into electricity, and a **motor** turns electricity into motion.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
Ohm's law, 'is a fuse in series or parallel', and 'what is electromagnetic induction the basis of' are standard statement MCQs; power formulae and the kilowatt-hour unit also recur.

**Picture it**

| Idea | Fact |
|---|---|
| Ohm's law | V = IR (voltage = current × resistance) |
| Series circuit | same current everywhere; resistances add |
| Parallel circuit | same voltage across each; used in homes |
| Electric power | P = VI = I²R = V² ÷ R; energy sold in kilowatt-hours ('units') |
| Fuse / MCB | in series in the live wire; works by the heating effect of current |

### Modern physics — inside the atom

**The story (continued)**
An atom is a tiny nucleus of **protons and neutrons** surrounded by electrons. Some heavy nuclei are unstable and shoot out radiation: **alpha** (a helium nucleus), **beta** (an electron) or **gamma** (high-energy light). Two processes release huge energy: **fission**, where a heavy nucleus is split into lighter pieces — this runs every nuclear power reactor and the atom bomb; and **fusion**, where light nuclei are squeezed together into a heavier one — this powers the Sun and the hydrogen bomb. Controlled fusion on Earth is still experimental (projects such as ITER), so reactors today use fission only.

**Picture it**

| Emission | What it is |
|---|---|
| Alpha | a helium nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons) |
| Beta | a fast electron |
| Gamma | high-energy electromagnetic radiation |

**Terms explained**
- **Current (I)** — the flow of electric charge, measured in amperes.
- **Resistance (R)** — opposition to current, measured in ohms.
- **Electromagnetic induction** — producing a current by moving a magnet near a coil (Faraday).
- **Fission** — splitting a heavy nucleus; **Fusion** — joining light nuclei.
- **Kilowatt-hour** — the commercial 'unit' of electrical energy on your bill.

**Don't confuse**
- **Fission vs fusion** — fission *splits* (reactors, atom bomb); fusion *joins* (the Sun, hydrogen bomb).
- **Fuse: series not parallel** — it must carry the full current to break it, so it sits in series.
- **Generator vs motor** — generator makes electricity from motion; motor makes motion from electricity.

**Remember it**
"Fu**S**ion = **S**un and **S**tars (joining); fi**SS**ion = **S**plitting."

**TL;DR**
- Ohm's law V = IR; power P = VI = I²R; energy billed in kilowatt-hours.
- Series = same current; homes are wired in parallel; a fuse sits in series on the live wire.
- Electromagnetic induction (Faraday) is the basis of the generator; a motor converts electricity to motion.
- Radioactive emissions: alpha (helium nucleus), beta (electron), gamma (EM radiation).
- Fission (splitting) powers reactors; fusion (joining) powers the Sun.
keyPoints: Ohm's law: V = IR; electric power P = VI = I²R; commercial energy unit = kilowatt-hour.
In series the current is the same; household appliances are wired in parallel.
A fuse/MCB is connected in series in the live wire and works on the heating effect of current.
Electromagnetic induction (Faraday) is the basis of the generator; a motor converts electrical to mechanical energy.
Radioactive emissions: alpha (He nucleus), beta (electron), gamma (EM radiation).
Fission (heavy nucleus splits) powers reactors; fusion (light nuclei combine) powers the Sun.

items.title: Chemistry I — Matter, Atoms, Acids-Bases & Common Compounds
items.body:
### Matter and the atom

**In one line**
All stuff around us is matter, which we sort into elements, compounds and mixtures, and the atom is the smallest building block that decides how each behaves.

**The story**
Matter exists as solid, liquid or gas; some solids skip the liquid stage and turn straight to vapour (**sublimation**, as with camphor and dry ice). We classify matter by what it is made of: an **element** is one kind of atom (iron, oxygen), a **compound** is two or more elements chemically joined in a fixed ratio (water, carbon dioxide), and a **mixture** is substances merely mixed with no fixed ratio (air, sea water). A change that makes no new substance is **physical** (ice melting); one that makes a new substance is **chemical** (iron rusting, wood burning). Zoom in and every element is made of atoms: a nucleus of **protons** (which set the atomic number) and **neutrons**, circled by electrons. Atoms of the same element with different neutron counts are **isotopes** — same atomic number, different mass number.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
'Is air a compound or mixture?', 'is rusting physical or chemical?', atomic-number/mass-number definitions and the chemical names of household compounds are high-frequency APPSC items.

**Picture it**

| Type | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Element | one kind of atom | iron, oxygen, gold |
| Compound | elements chemically joined | water, carbon dioxide, common salt |
| Mixture | just mixed, no fixed ratio | air, sea water, soil |

### Acids, bases and common compounds

**The story (continued)**
Acids taste sour and release hydrogen ions; bases feel soapy and release hydroxide ions. The **pH scale** from 0 to 14 measures this: below 7 is acidic, exactly 7 is neutral (pure water), above 7 is basic. When an acid meets a base they cancel out — **neutralisation** — giving a salt and water. Many everyday substances are simple salts and compounds with well-known chemical names, and APPSC loves matching the common name to the formula.

**Picture it**

| Common name | Chemical name / formula |
|---|---|
| Common salt | sodium chloride, NaCl |
| Baking soda | sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO₃ |
| Washing soda | hydrated sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O |
| Bleaching powder | calcium oxychloride, CaOCl₂ |
| Quicklime | calcium oxide, CaO |
| Slaked lime | calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂ |
| Plaster of Paris | calcium sulphate hemihydrate, CaSO₄·½H₂O |

**Terms explained**
- **Atomic number** — the number of protons in an atom; it defines the element.
- **Mass number** — protons plus neutrons.
- **Isotopes** — atoms of one element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers (carbon-12 and carbon-14).
- **Valency** — an atom's combining capacity (carbon's valency is 4, giving methane, CH₄).
- **pH** — a 0-to-14 number showing how acidic (<7) or basic (>7) a solution is.

**Don't confuse**
- **Air vs water** — air is a *mixture*; water is a *compound*.
- **Physical vs chemical change** — melting is physical (no new substance); rusting and burning are chemical.
- **Isotopes keep atomic number** — they differ in mass number (neutrons), not atomic number.
- **Baking soda vs washing soda** — baking soda is NaHCO₃; washing soda is Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.

**Remember it**
"**Baking** soda = **bi**carbonate (NaHCO₃)"; and "pH **l**ow = acid, pH **h**igh = base".

**TL;DR**
- Air is a mixture; water and carbon dioxide are compounds; rusting and burning are chemical changes.
- Atomic number = protons; mass number = protons + neutrons; isotopes share atomic number.
- Valency = combining capacity; carbon's is 4.
- pH below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic; acid + base → salt + water.
- Baking soda NaHCO₃, washing soda Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, bleaching powder CaOCl₂, quicklime CaO.
keyPoints: Air is a mixture; water and CO₂ are compounds; rusting and burning are chemical changes.
Atomic number = protons; mass number = protons + neutrons; isotopes share atomic number, differ in mass.
Valency = combining capacity; carbon has valency 4.
pH < 7 acidic, 7 neutral, > 7 basic; acid + base → salt + water (neutralisation).
Baking soda = NaHCO₃, washing soda = Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, bleaching powder = CaOCl₂, quicklime = CaO.
Plaster of Paris = CaSO₄·½H₂O; slaked lime = Ca(OH)₂; common salt = NaCl.

items.title: Chemistry II — Metals, Non-metals, Carbon Compounds & Fertilisers
items.body:
### Metals, non-metals and alloys

**In one line**
Metals are shiny, bendable conductors; non-metals are mostly dull insulators; mixing metals gives alloys with better properties.

**The story**
Metals shine, can be hammered into sheets (malleable) and drawn into wires (ductile), and conduct heat and electricity; **mercury** is the odd one out — the only metal that is liquid at room temperature. Non-metals are generally brittle and poor conductors, with **graphite** the famous exception that conducts. The **noble (inert) gases** — helium, neon, argon and others — barely react, which is why an electric filament bulb is filled with **argon or nitrogen**: an unreactive atmosphere stops the white-hot tungsten filament from reacting with oxygen and burning out. Metals can be ranked by how eagerly they react (the **reactivity series**); gold and silver sit at the unreactive end, so they are called noble metals. Because a pure metal is not always ideal, we blend metals into **alloys** — brass, bronze and steel each gain strength or resistance from the mix.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
'Only liquid metal', alloy compositions, 'which gas fills a bulb and why', and the reactivity order are repeat APPSC single-fact and statement questions.

**Picture it**

| Alloy | Made from |
|---|---|
| Brass | copper + zinc |
| Bronze | copper + tin |
| Steel | iron + carbon |
| Stainless steel | iron + chromium + nickel |

Reactivity series (most to least reactive): K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag > Au.

### Carbon compounds and fertilisers

**The story (continued)**
Carbon is special because it bonds with itself in long chains, so it forms millions of compounds. The same element can appear in different physical forms, called **allotropes**: diamond (hardest natural substance), graphite (soft and conducting), fullerene and graphene. **Hydrocarbons** are compounds of only carbon and hydrogen — methane (CH₄) is the simplest. **Polymers** are very long repeating chains: some are natural (cellulose, natural rubber, proteins), others synthetic (polythene, PVC, nylon, bakelite). Crops need three main nutrients, remembered as **NPK** — nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium; urea is the main nitrogen fertiliser.

**Terms explained**
- **Malleable** — can be hammered into thin sheets.
- **Ductile** — can be drawn into wires.
- **Alloy** — a mixture of a metal with other metals or carbon to improve its properties.
- **Allotropes** — different physical forms of the same element (diamond and graphite are both carbon).
- **Polymer** — a large molecule made of many repeating small units.

**Don't confuse**
- **Natural vs synthetic polymer** — cellulose and natural rubber are natural; polythene, PVC and nylon are synthetic.
- **Brass vs bronze** — brass is copper + zinc; bronze is copper + tin.
- **Diamond vs graphite** — same element (carbon), opposite properties: diamond is hard and non-conducting, graphite is soft and conducting.

**Remember it**
"**Bra**ss has **z**inc (Bra-Z); **bro**nze has **t**in"; crops want "**NPK** — Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Potassium".

**TL;DR**
- Mercury is the only liquid metal; non-metals are poor conductors except graphite.
- Filament bulbs are filled with argon (or nitrogen) to stop the filament oxidising.
- Reactivity series: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag > Au; gold and silver are noble.
- Brass = copper + zinc; bronze = copper + tin; steel = iron + carbon.
- Carbon allotropes diamond/graphite/fullerene/graphene; methane is the simplest hydrocarbon; fertilisers supply N-P-K (urea = nitrogen).
keyPoints: Mercury is the only metal liquid at room temperature; non-metals are poor conductors (except graphite).
Electric filament bulbs are filled with argon (or nitrogen), an inert gas, to prevent the filament from oxidising.
Reactivity series: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag > Au; gold and silver are noble metals.
Brass = copper + zinc; bronze = copper + tin; steel = iron + carbon.
Carbon allotropes: diamond, graphite, fullerene, graphene; methane is the simplest hydrocarbon.
Polythene, PVC and nylon are synthetic polymers; cellulose and natural rubber are natural polymers.
Fertilisers supply N-P-K; urea is a nitrogenous fertiliser.

items.title: Biology — Cell, Human Body, Nutrition & Plant Physiology
items.body:
### The cell and the human body

**In one line**
The cell is the basic unit of all life, and the human body is a team of organ systems each with its own working unit.

**The story**
Robert Hooke first saw box-like 'cells' in cork; later Robert Brown spotted the **nucleus**, the cell's control centre. Inside the cell, the **mitochondria** release energy and so are called the powerhouse, while ribosomes build proteins. Plant and animal cells differ in a few key parts — a plant cell has a rigid cell wall and green chloroplasts, which animal cells lack. In the body, each system has a basic unit and a headline fact worth memorising: the **neuron** is the basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system, the **medulla oblongata** (lowest part of the brain) controls involuntary actions such as heartbeat and breathing, the **nephron** is the functional unit of the kidney and filters urea out of the blood (the liver *makes* urea; the kidney *removes* it), the lungs' **alveoli** exchange gases, and the **liver** is the largest gland. Blood comes in groups, with **O-negative** the universal donor and **AB** the universal recipient.

**Why it matters / why it is asked**
'Powerhouse of the cell', 'largest gland', universal donor/recipient, and functional units (neuron, nephron) are among the most repeated science facts in APPSC and other PSC papers.

**Picture it**

| Feature | Plant cell | Animal cell |
|---|---|---|
| Cell wall | present | absent |
| Chloroplast | present | absent |
| Large vacuole | present | small or absent |

### Nutrition, hormones and plants

**The story (continued)**
Food supplies vitamins, and a shortage of each causes a specific **deficiency disease** — these matches are classic exam fodder. Chemical messengers called **hormones** keep the body balanced: insulin from the pancreas controls blood sugar, thyroxine from the thyroid controls metabolism (it needs iodine, and a shortage causes goitre), adrenaline is the fight-or-flight hormone, and the pituitary at the base of the brain is the 'master gland'. Green plants make their own food by **photosynthesis** — using sunlight, the green pigment chlorophyll turns carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen — and lose excess water as vapour through tiny leaf pores (**transpiration**). All living things are sorted by Whittaker's **five-kingdom** scheme.

**Picture it**

| Deficiency | Disease |
|---|---|
| Vitamin A | night blindness |
| Vitamin C | scurvy |
| Vitamin D | rickets |
| Vitamin B1 | beriberi |
| Iron | anaemia |
| Iodine | goitre |

**Terms explained**
- **Nucleus** — the control centre of the cell that holds its genetic material.
- **Mitochondria** — the cell's powerhouse, where energy is released.
- **Nephron** — the filtering unit of the kidney.
- **Hormone** — a chemical messenger released by a gland into the blood.
- **Photosynthesis** — how green plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight and chlorophyll.

**Don't confuse**
- **Cell wall vs cell membrane** — the rigid cell wall is only in plant cells; both plant and animal cells have a membrane.
- **Largest gland vs pancreas** — the liver is the largest gland; the pancreas is the second largest.
- **Neuron vs nephron** — neuron is the nerve unit; nephron is the kidney unit.
- **Universal donor vs recipient** — O-negative donates to all; AB receives from all.

**Remember it**
"**Mito**chondria = **might** (power) house"; five kingdoms spell **MPFPA** — Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.

**TL;DR**
- Robert Hooke saw cells; Robert Brown found the nucleus; mitochondria = powerhouse.
- Plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts; animal cells lack both.
- Liver is the largest gland; alveoli exchange gases; O-negative = universal donor, AB = universal recipient.
- Deficiencies: Vitamin A → night blindness, C → scurvy, D → rickets, B1 → beriberi, iron → anaemia, iodine → goitre.
- Photosynthesis needs chlorophyll and sunlight; Whittaker's five kingdoms are Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
keyPoints: Robert Hooke discovered cells (cork); Robert Brown discovered the nucleus; mitochondria = powerhouse.
Plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts; animal cells lack both.
Liver is the largest gland; alveoli exchange gases; O-negative = universal donor, AB = universal recipient.
Neuron = nervous system unit; nephron = kidney unit; medulla controls heartbeat and breathing.

Photosynthesis needs chlorophyll and light; Whittaker's five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.

items.title: Physics IV — SI Units, Special Units, Instruments & Temperature
items.body:
## Units and measuring instruments

**In one line:** every quantity has an agreed unit, and every everyday measurement has a named instrument.

**Why it is asked:** "SI unit of X", "light year is a unit of?" and "instrument → what it measures" are among the most repeated one-line science items in APPSC and other PSC papers.

**The story**

The seven **base** units (metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela) are the foundation; every other unit is **derived** from them and many are named after scientists — the newton after Isaac Newton, the volt after Alessandro Volta, the ohm after Georg Ohm. Some units look like time but are not: a **light year** is a *distance*. Instruments are named from Greek roots: *baro* = weight (of air), *hygro* = wet, *lacto* = milk, *anemo* = wind, *seismo* = shaking.

### Seven SI base units

| Quantity | SI base unit |
|---|---|
| **Length** | metre (m) |
| **Mass** | kilogram (kg) |
| **Time** | second (s) |
| **Electric current** | ampere (A) |
| **Thermodynamic temperature** | kelvin (K) |
| **Amount of substance** | mole (mol) |
| **Luminous intensity** | candela (cd) |

### Derived SI units (named after scientists)

| Quantity | SI unit |
|---|---|
| **Force** | newton (N) |
| **Work and energy** | joule (J) |
| **Power** | watt (W) |
| **Pressure** | pascal (Pa) |
| **Frequency** | hertz (Hz) |
| **Electric charge** | coulomb (C) |
| **Potential difference (voltage)** | volt (V) |
| **Electrical resistance** | ohm (Ω) |
| **Magnetic flux** | weber (Wb) |
| **Magnetic field (flux density)** | tesla (T) |
| **Capacitance** | farad (F) |
| **Radioactivity** | becquerel (Bq) |
| **Power of a lens** | dioptre (D) |
| **Sound intensity level (loudness)** | decibel (dB) |

### Special and practical units

| Unit | What it measures / equals |
|---|---|
| **Light year** | distance travelled by light in one year (about 9.46 × 10^{12} km) |
| **Astronomical unit (AU)** | mean Earth–Sun distance (about 1.496 × 10^{8} km) |
| **Parsec** | about 3.26 light years (largest practical unit of distance) |
| **Angstrom** | 10^{-10} metre (used for wavelengths and atomic sizes) |
| **Nautical mile** | 1,852 metres (sea and air navigation) |
| **Knot** | speed of one nautical mile per hour (ships, aircraft) |
| **Fathom** | six feet — unit of depth of water |
| **Kilowatt-hour (kWh)** | commercial unit of electrical energy = 3.6 × 10^{6} joules |
| **Calorie** | heat needed to raise 1 g of water by 1 °C (about 4.18 joules) |
| **Mach number** | speed of a body divided by the speed of sound (above 1 = supersonic) |

### Measuring instruments

| Instrument | What it measures |
|---|---|
| **Barometer** | atmospheric pressure |
| **Hygrometer** | relative humidity of the air |
| **Lactometer** | purity (density) of milk |
| **Anemometer** | wind speed |
| **Seismograph** | earthquake waves (intensity of earthquakes) |
| **Sphygmomanometer** | blood pressure |
| **Ammeter** | electric current (connected in series) |
| **Voltmeter** | potential difference (connected in parallel) |
| **Galvanometer** | detects small electric currents |
| **Odometer** | distance travelled by a vehicle |
| **Altimeter** | altitude (height) of an aircraft |
| **Pyrometer** | very high temperatures (furnaces) |
| **Fathometer** | depth of the sea (uses echo) |
| **Thermostat** | keeps a temperature constant automatically |
| **Tachometer** | rotation speed of an engine shaft (rpm) |
| **Audiometer** | hearing ability (sound intensity) |
| **Manometer** | pressure of gases |
| **Rain gauge (udometer)** | amount of rainfall |
| **Stethoscope** | heart and lung sounds |

### Temperature scales — key values

| Point | Value |
|---|---|
| **Same reading on Celsius and Fahrenheit** | −40 degrees |
| **Absolute zero** | 0 K = −273.15 °C |
| **Normal human body temperature** | 37 °C = 98.6 °F |
| **Boiling point of water at sea level** | 100 °C = 212 °F = 373 K |
| **Celsius to Fahrenheit** | F = (9/5) × C + 32 |

## Don't confuse
- **Light year** is a unit of **distance**, not time; the **parsec** (about 3.26 light years) is even larger.
- **Hydrometer** = density of any liquid; **hygrometer** = humidity of air; **lactometer** = milk only.
- **Ammeter** goes in **series**; **voltmeter** goes in **parallel**.
- **Kilowatt-hour** is a unit of **energy** (the "unit" on your bill), not of power.

**Remember it:** "Baro-pressure, Hygro-humidity, Anemo-wind, Seismo-quake, Lacto-milk."

**TL;DR**
- Seven base units: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela.
- Light year = distance; 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10^{6} J; 1 nautical mile = 1,852 m.
- −40 is the same on Celsius and Fahrenheit; absolute zero = −273.15 °C; body = 37 °C = 98.6 °F.
keyPoints: Length — metre (m).
Mass — kilogram (kg).
Force — newton (N).
Work and energy — joule (J).
Light year — distance travelled by light in one year (about 9.46 × 10^{12} km).
Kilowatt-hour (kWh) — commercial unit of electrical energy = 3.6 × 10^{6} joules.
Barometer — atmospheric pressure.
Hygrometer — relative humidity of the air.

items.title: Physics V — Named Laws, Principles & Everyday Mechanics
items.body:
## Named laws and principles of physics

**In one line:** most "which principle explains this?" questions map an everyday device to one named law.

**Why it is asked:** hydraulic brakes (Pascal), aeroplane lift (Bernoulli), rocket and gun recoil (Newton's third law / momentum), seat belts (inertia) and raindrops (surface tension) are favourite application MCQs.

**The story**

Pascal saw that pressure pushed into a closed liquid spreads equally everywhere, so a small push on a small piston lifts a car on a big one. Bernoulli found that where a fluid flows faster its pressure drops — air over a curved wing moves faster, so the wing is pushed up. Newton's laws explain why a passenger lurches forward when a bus brakes (inertia) and why a rocket rises when gas is thrown down (action–reaction).

### Laws and principles — what they say and where they are used

| Law / principle | Statement or application |
|---|---|
| **Pascal's law** | pressure on an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions — hydraulic lift, press and brakes |
| **Bernoulli's principle** | faster-moving fluid has lower pressure — lift on aeroplane wings, roofs blown off in storms |
| **Boyle's law** | at constant temperature the volume of a gas varies inversely with its pressure |
| **Charles's law** | at constant pressure the volume of a gas is proportional to its absolute temperature |
| **Avogadro's law** | equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules |
| **Hooke's law** | within the elastic limit stress is proportional to strain — the spring balance |
| **Kepler's first law** | planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus |
| **Newton's law of cooling** | rate of cooling is proportional to the temperature difference with the surroundings |
| **Coulomb's law** | force between two charges is proportional to their product and inversely to the square of the distance |
| **Joule's law of heating** | heat produced H = I²Rt — basis of the electric heater, iron and fuse |
| **Lenz's law** | an induced current always opposes the change that produced it |
| **Fleming's left-hand rule** | direction of force on a current-carrying conductor — electric motor |
| **Fleming's right-hand rule** | direction of induced current — electric generator |
| **Snell's law** | law of refraction: sin i ÷ sin r is a constant (the refractive index) |
| **Doppler effect** | apparent change in frequency when source and observer move relative to each other — police speed radar, red shift of galaxies |
| **Tyndall effect** | scattering of light by colloidal particles — a beam visible in a dusty room or misty forest |
| **Photoelectric effect** | emission of electrons when light falls on a metal — explained by Einstein (Nobel Prize 1921); basis of solar cells |
| **Heisenberg's uncertainty principle** | position and momentum of a particle cannot both be known exactly at the same time |

### Everyday mechanics — which idea explains it

| Everyday observation | Explained by |
|---|---|
| **Passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly (seat belts needed)** | inertia of motion (Newton's first law) |
| **Dust leaves a carpet when it is beaten** | inertia of rest |
| **A gun recoils when fired** | conservation of momentum (Newton's third law) |
| **A rocket rises by throwing hot gases downward** | Newton's third law (action and reaction) |
| **Raindrops are spherical; insects walk on water** | surface tension |
| **Oil rises up a lamp wick; blotting paper soaks ink** | capillarity (capillary action) |
| **Honey flows more slowly than water** | viscosity (internal friction of a fluid) |
| **Roads and railway tracks are banked at curves** | centripetal force needed for circular motion |
| **Escape velocity from Earth** | about 11.2 km per second |
| **Orbital velocity of a satellite close to Earth** | about 7.9 km per second |

## Don't confuse
- **Pascal** = pressure spreads equally (hydraulics); **Bernoulli** = faster flow, lower pressure (lift).
- **Boyle** = constant temperature (P and V inverse); **Charles** = constant pressure (V and T direct).
- **Left-hand rule = motor; right-hand rule = generator.**
- **Escape velocity** (11.2 km/s) is larger than **orbital velocity** (about 7.9 km/s).

**Remember it:** "Pascal pushes brakes, Bernoulli lifts planes, Newton fires rockets."

**TL;DR**
- Hydraulic brakes = Pascal; aeroplane lift = Bernoulli; spring balance = Hooke.
- Doppler = frequency shift (speed radar); photoelectric effect = Einstein, solar cells.
- Seat belt = inertia; gun recoil = momentum; rocket = third law; raindrop = surface tension.
keyPoints: Pascal's law — pressure on an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions — hydraulic lift, press and brakes.
Bernoulli's principle — faster-moving fluid has lower pressure — lift on aeroplane wings, roofs blown off in storms.
Passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly (seat belts needed) — inertia of motion (Newton's first law).
A gun recoils when fired — conservation of momentum (Newton's third law).

items.title: Physics VI — Light Phenomena, Eye Defects & the Electromagnetic Spectrum
items.body:
## Why the sky is blue and how the eye is corrected

**In one line:** scattering, refraction and total internal reflection explain almost every natural light phenomenon; lenses correct the eye.

**Why it is asked:** "why is the sky blue / danger signal red / stars twinkle / diamond sparkle" and "lens for myopia" are evergreen statement and match items.

**The story**

Light travels at about 3 × 10^{8} m/s and takes roughly 8 minutes 20 seconds to arrive from the Sun. Tiny air molecules scatter short (blue) wavelengths far more than long (red) ones, so the sky looks blue and red signals carry farthest. When light tries to leave a dense medium at a steep angle it is totally reflected back — **total internal reflection** — which makes diamonds sparkle and lets optical fibres carry signals.

### Light phenomena and their cause

| Phenomenon | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Blue colour of the sky** | scattering of light (blue scattered most) |
| **Red colour for danger signals** | red is scattered least (longest wavelength), so it is seen from far |
| **Reddish Sun at sunrise and sunset** | blue light scattered away over the long path through air |
| **Twinkling of stars** | atmospheric refraction |
| **Planets do not twinkle** | they are near and look like extended discs, not points |
| **Sun seen about 2 minutes before actual sunrise** | atmospheric refraction |
| **Mirage in deserts and on hot roads** | total internal reflection (with refraction) in hot air layers |
| **Sparkling of a diamond** | total internal reflection (very high refractive index of diamond) |
| **Optical fibre carrying signals** | total internal reflection of light along the glass core |
| **Rainbow** | dispersion, refraction and internal reflection in raindrops (seen opposite the Sun) |
| **Pool looks shallower; pencil looks bent in water** | refraction |

### Light — key numbers and facts

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Speed of light in vacuum** | about 3 × 10^{8} metres per second |
| **Time for sunlight to reach Earth** | about 8 minutes 20 seconds |
| **Primary colours of light** | red, green and blue |
| **Periscope** | two plane mirrors (or prisms) at 45 degrees |
| **Kaleidoscope** | multiple reflection between inclined plane mirrors |
| **Dentist's and shaving mirror; solar cooker** | concave mirror |

### The human eye and its defects

| Defect / part | Fact or correction |
|---|---|
| **Myopia (short-sightedness)** | far objects blurred; corrected with a concave lens |
| **Hypermetropia (long-sightedness)** | near objects blurred; corrected with a convex lens |
| **Presbyopia** | age-related loss of focusing power; corrected with bifocal lenses |
| **Astigmatism** | unequal curvature of the cornea; corrected with a cylindrical lens |
| **Cataract** | eye lens becomes cloudy (opaque); treated by surgery |
| **Retina** | light-sensitive screen where a real, inverted image forms |
| **Rods and cones** | rods sense dim light; cones sense colour |
| **Iris** | controls the size of the pupil |
| **Power of a lens** | P = 1 ÷ focal length in metres; convex lens positive, concave negative |

### Electromagnetic spectrum — uses

| Radiation | Key fact or use |
|---|---|
| **Gamma rays** | shortest wavelength, most penetrating; cancer treatment |
| **X-rays** | imaging of bones; discovered by Wilhelm Röntgen (1895) |
| **Ultraviolet rays** | make vitamin D in skin, kill germs; mostly absorbed by the ozone layer |
| **Infrared rays** | heat radiation; TV remote controls and night-vision devices |
| **Microwaves** | radar and microwave ovens |
| **Radio waves** | longest wavelength; radio and TV broadcasting |

## Don't confuse
- **Twinkling** = atmospheric **refraction**; **blue sky** = **scattering**; **diamond, mirage, optical fibre** = **total internal reflection**.
- **Myopia → concave lens**; **hypermetropia → convex lens**; **astigmatism → cylindrical**; **presbyopia → bifocal**.
- **Gamma** has the shortest wavelength; **radio** the longest.

**Remember it:** "My-Concave (myopia–concave), Hyper-Convex."

**TL;DR**
- Speed of light about 3 × 10^{8} m/s; sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds.
- Blue sky and red signals = scattering; twinkling = refraction; sparkle and fibre = total internal reflection.
- UV makes vitamin D and is stopped by ozone; infrared = remotes and night vision; X-rays = bones.
keyPoints: Blue colour of the sky — scattering of light (blue scattered most).
Red colour for danger signals — red is scattered least (longest wavelength), so it is seen from far.
Speed of light in vacuum — about 3 × 10^{8} metres per second.
Myopia (short-sightedness) — far objects blurred; corrected with a concave lens.
Hypermetropia (long-sightedness) — near objects blurred; corrected with a convex lens.
Gamma rays — shortest wavelength, most penetrating; cancer treatment.
X-rays — imaging of bones; discovered by Wilhelm Röntgen (1895).

items.title: Physics VII — Sound & Heat in Everyday Life
items.body:
## Sound and heat — the applied facts

**In one line:** pitch, loudness and echo explain how we hear; expansion, evaporation and boiling-point rules explain everyday heat effects.

**Why it is asked:** "pitch depends on?", "why lakes freeze from the top", "why cooking is hard in the hills" and "why a matka cools water" are standard one-liners.

**The story**

A sound's **pitch** (shrill or deep) is set by its frequency, while its **loudness** is set by how big the vibration is (its amplitude). Water behaves oddly: it is densest at **4 °C**, so in winter the coldest water floats to the top and freezes, and fish survive below. Boiling depends on the air pressure above a liquid — lower pressure in the hills means water boils below 100 °C, which is why a pressure cooker (which raises the pressure) cooks faster.

### Sound — characteristics and uses

| Feature | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Pitch (shrillness)** | depends on frequency — a woman's voice usually has higher pitch |
| **Loudness** | depends on amplitude; measured in decibels |
| **Quality (timbre)** | depends on waveform — lets us tell instruments apart |
| **Speed of sound in water** | about 1,500 metres per second (over four times faster than in air) |
| **Speed of sound and temperature** | speed of sound increases with temperature and humidity |
| **Echo** | heard only if the reflector is at least about 17.2 m away (0.1 s gap) |
| **Sound waves in air** | longitudinal waves of compressions and rarefactions |
| **Bats and dolphins** | use ultrasound to locate objects (echolocation) |
| **Elephants and whales** | communicate using infrasound |
| **Ultrasound in medicine** | sonography of the foetus and organs; breaking kidney stones |
| **Sonic boom** | shock wave when a body moves faster than sound (supersonic) |
| **Reverberation** | persistence of sound by repeated reflections in a large hall |

### Heat in everyday life

| Observation | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Water is densest at 4 °C** | anomalous expansion — lakes freeze from the top and fish survive below |
| **Cooking is difficult at high altitude** | lower air pressure lowers the boiling point of water |
| **A pressure cooker cooks faster** | higher pressure raises the boiling point of water |
| **Water stays cool in an earthen pot (matka); sweating cools us** | evaporation causes cooling |
| **Thermos (vacuum) flask** | vacuum stops conduction and convection; silvered walls stop radiation |
| **Black surfaces get hot; white clothes are worn in summer** | black is the best absorber and emitter of heat |
| **Gaps are left between railway rails** | thermal expansion in summer |
| **Ice melts under pressure and refreezes (ice skating)** | regelation — pressure lowers the melting point of ice |
| **Bimetallic strip in a thermostat** | two metals expand unequally and the strip bends |

## Don't confuse
- **Pitch = frequency; loudness = amplitude.**
- **Altitude lowers** the boiling point; a **pressure cooker raises** it.
- **Ultrasound** = bats, dolphins, SONAR, sonography; **infrasound** = elephants, whales, earthquakes.

**Remember it:** "Four-degree water floats no more — it sinks, so lakes freeze from the top."

**TL;DR**
- Pitch ∝ frequency; loudness ∝ amplitude (decibel); echo needs about 17.2 m.
- Sound travels about 1,500 m/s in water; speed rises with temperature.
- Water densest at 4 °C; evaporation cools; altitude lowers boiling point; pressure cooker raises it.
keyPoints: Pitch (shrillness) — depends on frequency — a woman's voice usually has higher pitch.
Loudness — depends on amplitude; measured in decibels.
Water is densest at 4 °C — anomalous expansion — lakes freeze from the top and fish survive below.
Cooking is difficult at high altitude — lower air pressure lowers the boiling point of water.

items.title: Physics VIII — Electricity & Magnetism in Daily Life
items.body:
## Household electricity, materials and magnets

**In one line:** which material is used where (tungsten, nichrome, copper, silicon), how household supply works and what each electrical device converts.

**Why it is asked:** "filament is made of?", "heating element is made of?", "India's AC frequency", "transformer works on?" and "LED vs CFL" are repeat PSC items.

**The story**

Indian homes receive **alternating current (AC)** at about **220–230 volts and 50 hertz**. A **transformer** steps this voltage up or down using mutual induction, so it works only on AC. Materials are chosen for one property: **tungsten** for bulb filaments because it melts only at about 3,400 °C, **nichrome** for heater coils because it has high resistance and does not oxidise easily, and **silver** is the best conductor although **copper** is cheaper and used in wiring. **Silicon and germanium** are semiconductors — the heart of diodes, transistors and solar cells.

### Electricity — materials, devices and supply

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Household supply in India** | AC at about 220–230 volts and 50 hertz |
| **Transformer** | steps AC voltage up or down; works only on AC (mutual induction) |
| **Heating element of heaters and irons** | nichrome (nickel–chromium alloy) |
| **Filament of an incandescent bulb** | tungsten (melting point about 3,400 °C) |
| **Fuse wire** | alloy of tin and lead with a low melting point |
| **Best conductor of electricity** | silver (copper is used in wiring as it is cheaper) |
| **Semiconductors** | silicon and germanium |
| **Colour code of house wires** | live — red or brown; neutral — black or blue; earth — green |
| **LED lamp versus CFL** | LED is more energy-efficient and has no mercury; a CFL contains mercury |
| **Diode** | lets current flow one way — used as a rectifier (AC to DC) |
| **Transistor** | amplifier and electronic switch |
| **Electric cell (battery)** | chemical energy to electrical energy; gives DC (Volta made the first cell) |
| **Solar (photovoltaic) cell** | light energy to electrical energy; made of silicon |
| **Superconductor** | zero electrical resistance at very low temperatures |
| **Resistance of a wire** | increases with length and decreases with thickness (cross-section area) |
| **Lightning conductor** | pointed copper rod that leads charge to earth (Benjamin Franklin) |

### Magnetism

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Hans Christian Oersted (1820)** | showed that an electric current produces a magnetic field |
| **Michael Faraday (1831)** | discovered electromagnetic induction (basis of the generator and transformer) |
| **Core of an electromagnet** | soft iron (magnetises and demagnetises easily) |
| **Permanent magnets** | steel or alloys such as alnico |
| **Earth as a magnet** | Earth's geographic north is near its magnetic south pole, so a compass needle points north |
| **Magnetic poles** | like poles repel, unlike poles attract |

## Don't confuse
- **Tungsten** = bulb filament (very high melting point); **nichrome** = heater element (high resistance); **tin–lead** = fuse wire (low melting point).
- **Transformer** works on **AC only**; a **cell** gives **DC**.
- **Silver** is the best conductor; **copper** is used for wiring because it is cheaper.

**Remember it:** "Tungsten Toughs out heat, Nichrome makes heat, Fuse Fails first."

**TL;DR**
- Indian supply: AC, about 220–230 V, 50 Hz; earth wire green.
- Semiconductors silicon and germanium; diode = rectifier; solar cell = light to electricity.
- Faraday (1831) = electromagnetic induction; Oersted (1820) = current makes a magnetic field.
- LED: no mercury, more efficient; CFL contains mercury.
keyPoints: Household supply in India — AC at about 220–230 volts and 50 hertz.
Transformer — steps AC voltage up or down; works only on AC (mutual induction).
Michael Faraday (1831) — discovered electromagnetic induction (basis of the generator and transformer).

items.title: Physics IX — Discoveries of the Atom, Radioactivity & Isotope Uses
items.body:
## Who found what inside the atom

**In one line:** the electron, proton, neutron and nucleus were each discovered by a named scientist, and radioactive isotopes have fixed uses in medicine and dating.

**Why it is asked:** "neutron was discovered by?", "radioactivity discovered by?", "isotope used for carbon dating / thyroid / cancer" and "moderator in a reactor" are standard PSC items.

**The story**

In 1897 **J.J. Thomson** found the electron in cathode rays. **Rutherford** fired alpha particles at gold foil (1911) and found a tiny, dense, positive **nucleus**. **James Chadwick** found the neutron in 1932. Earlier, in 1896, **Henri Becquerel** found that uranium gives off radiation on its own — radioactivity — and **Marie and Pierre Curie** went on to discover polonium and radium. In a reactor, **heavy water** slows neutrons (a moderator) and **cadmium or boron** rods soak them up to control the chain reaction.

### Discoveries in atomic physics

| Discovery | Scientist |
|---|---|
| **Electron (1897)** | J.J. Thomson |
| **Proton (canal rays, 1886)** | E. Goldstein (named by Rutherford) |
| **Neutron (1932)** | James Chadwick |
| **Nucleus — gold-foil (alpha scattering) experiment, 1911** | Ernest Rutherford |
| **Electrons in fixed orbits (shells), 1913** | Niels Bohr |
| **Radioactivity (1896)** | Henri Becquerel |
| **Polonium and radium** | Marie and Pierre Curie |
| **X-rays (1895)** | Wilhelm Röntgen — first Nobel Prize in Physics, 1901 |
| **Mass–energy equivalence E = mc²** | Albert Einstein |
| **Nuclear fission (1938)** | Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann |

### Radioactivity and isotopes — uses and facts

| Item | Fact or use |
|---|---|
| **Penetrating power of radiations** | gamma > beta > alpha (alpha is stopped by paper) |
| **Half-life** | time in which half the nuclei of a radioactive sample decay |
| **Carbon-14** | radiocarbon dating of fossils and archaeological remains |
| **Cobalt-60** | radiotherapy of cancer |
| **Iodine-131** | diagnosis and treatment of thyroid disorders |
| **Uranium-235** | fuel of nuclear fission reactors |
| **Heavy water (D₂O)** | moderator that slows neutrons in nuclear reactors |
| **Control rods** | cadmium or boron rods that absorb neutrons |
| **Isotopes of hydrogen** | protium, deuterium and tritium (tritium is radioactive) |
| **Isobars** | same mass number, different atomic numbers (argon-40 and calcium-40) |

## Don't confuse
- **Thomson = electron; Chadwick = neutron; Rutherford = nucleus; Goldstein = proton (canal rays).**
- **Becquerel** discovered radioactivity; the **Curies** discovered polonium and radium.
- **Isotopes** share atomic number; **isobars** share mass number.
- **Heavy water** is a **moderator** (slows neutrons); **cadmium/boron** rods **absorb** neutrons.

**Remember it:** "C-14 dates, Co-60 treats cancer, I-131 treats thyroid."

**TL;DR**
- Electron 1897 Thomson; nucleus 1911 Rutherford; neutron 1932 Chadwick; radioactivity 1896 Becquerel.
- Penetrating power gamma > beta > alpha.
- Heavy water = moderator; U-235 = fuel; C-14 = dating; Co-60 = cancer; I-131 = thyroid.
keyPoints: Electron (1897) — J.J. Thomson.
Neutron (1932) — James Chadwick.
Penetrating power of radiations — gamma > beta > alpha (alpha is stopped by paper).
Carbon-14 — radiocarbon dating of fossils and archaeological remains.

items.title: Chemistry III — Periodic Table, Abundance Records & Noble Gases
items.body:
## The periodic table and "the most / the only" records

**In one line:** the periodic table sorts elements by atomic number into 18 groups and 7 periods, and a handful of superlatives (most abundant, lightest, only liquid) are asked again and again.

**Why it is asked:** "Mendeleev arranged elements by?", "most abundant metal in the Earth's crust", "liquid non-metal" and "gas used in balloons" are classic PSC one-liners.

**The story**

**Mendeleev (1869)** arranged the then-known elements by **atomic mass** and left gaps for undiscovered ones. **Henry Moseley (1913)** showed that **atomic number** is the true basis — the modern periodic law. Today's table has **118 elements** in **18 groups** (columns) and **7 periods** (rows). Group 1 holds the reactive alkali metals, group 17 the halogens, group 18 the unreactive noble gases.

### The periodic table

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Mendeleev's periodic table (1869)** | elements arranged by atomic mass |
| **Modern periodic law (Moseley, 1913)** | elements arranged by atomic number |
| **Modern periodic table** | 18 groups and 7 periods |
| **Number of known elements** | 118 |
| **Group 1** | alkali metals (sodium, potassium) |
| **Group 17** | halogens (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine) |
| **Group 18** | noble (inert) gases |
| **Döbereiner's triads and Newlands' law of octaves** | early attempts at classifying elements |

### Element records (most, lightest, only)

| Record | Element |
|---|---|
| **Most abundant element in the Earth's crust** | oxygen (silicon is second) |
| **Most abundant metal in the Earth's crust** | aluminium |
| **Most abundant gas in the atmosphere** | nitrogen (about 78%; oxygen about 21%, argon about 0.93%) |
| **Most abundant element in the universe** | hydrogen |
| **Lightest element; lightest metal** | hydrogen; lithium |
| **Only non-metal that is liquid at room temperature** | bromine (mercury is the only liquid metal) |
| **Most electronegative (most reactive non-metal)** | fluorine |
| **Metal that melts in the palm of the hand** | gallium (melting point about 30 °C) |

### Noble gases and their uses

| Gas | Use |
|---|---|
| **Helium** | filling weather balloons and airships (light, non-inflammable); with oxygen in deep-sea diving cylinders |
| **Neon** | glowing advertisement signs |
| **Argon** | filling electric filament bulbs (with nitrogen) |
| **Radon** | radioactive noble gas used in radiotherapy |
| **Xenon** | high-intensity lamps and camera flash tubes |

## Don't confuse
- **Mendeleev = atomic mass; Moseley = atomic number.**
- **Oxygen** is the most abundant **element** of the crust; **aluminium** the most abundant **metal**; **nitrogen** the most abundant gas of the **air**.
- **Mercury** = only liquid **metal**; **bromine** = only liquid **non-metal**.

**Remember it:** "OSA — Oxygen, Silicon, Aluminium: the crust's top three."

**TL;DR**
- 118 elements, 18 groups, 7 periods; group 1 alkali metals, 17 halogens, 18 noble gases.
- Air: nitrogen about 78%, oxygen about 21%, argon about 0.93%.
- Helium = balloons and diving; neon = signs; argon = bulbs.
keyPoints: Mendeleev's periodic table (1869) — elements arranged by atomic mass.
Modern periodic law (Moseley, 1913) — elements arranged by atomic number.
Most abundant element in the Earth's crust — oxygen (silicon is second).
Most abundant metal in the Earth's crust — aluminium.
Helium — filling weather balloons and airships (light, non-inflammable); with oxygen in deep-sea diving cylinders.
Neon — glowing advertisement signs.

items.title: Chemistry IV — Acids in Daily Life, Indicators, Gases & Common Names
items.body:
## The chemistry of the kitchen and the market

**In one line:** each sour food carries a named acid, indicators change colour with pH, and many substances have popular names that hide their chemistry.

**Why it is asked:** "acid in tamarind / vinegar / ant sting", "laughing gas", "LPG is mainly?", "Bhopal gas" and "milk of magnesia" are among the most-asked chemistry facts in state PSC papers.

**The story**

Sourness means acid: vinegar has acetic acid, lemons citric acid, tamarind tartaric acid, curd lactic acid. An ant sting injects **formic acid**, so rubbing a mild base (baking soda) eases it. When the stomach makes too much hydrochloric acid, an **antacid** such as milk of magnesia (magnesium hydroxide) neutralises it. Indicators show acid or base by colour: blue litmus turns red in acid and red litmus turns blue in base.

### Natural sources of acids

| Source | Acid |
|---|---|
| **Vinegar** | acetic (ethanoic) acid |
| **Lemon and orange** | citric acid |
| **Tamarind (and grapes)** | tartaric acid |
| **Curd and sour milk** | lactic acid |
| **Ant sting and nettle sting** | formic (methanoic) acid |
| **Tomato** | oxalic acid |
| **Apple** | malic acid |
| **Gastric juice of the stomach** | hydrochloric acid |
| **Rancid butter** | butyric acid |
| **Car (lead-acid) battery** | sulphuric acid |
| **Soda water and soft drinks** | carbonic acid |

### Indicators, antacids and acid facts

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Litmus** | natural indicator from lichens; acid turns blue litmus red, base turns red litmus blue |
| **Phenolphthalein** | colourless in acid, pink in base |
| **Methyl orange** | red in acid, yellow in base |
| **Turmeric** | turns reddish-brown in a base (soap) |
| **Milk of magnesia** | magnesium hydroxide — an antacid |
| **Aqua regia** | concentrated hydrochloric and nitric acids in a 3 : 1 ratio; dissolves gold and platinum |
| **Oil of vitriol ("king of chemicals")** | sulphuric acid |
| **Tooth decay** | starts when the pH in the mouth falls below about 5.5 |
| **Acidic soil** | treated with lime (quicklime or slaked lime) |
| **Acid rain** | rain with pH below about 5.6 (sulphur and nitrogen oxides) |

### Gases and fuels — common names

| Common name / event | Chemical |
|---|---|
| **Laughing gas** | nitrous oxide (N₂O) |
| **Dry ice** | solid carbon dioxide |
| **Marsh gas** | methane |
| **LPG (liquefied petroleum gas)** | mainly butane (with propane); ethyl mercaptan is added for smell |
| **CNG (compressed natural gas)** | mainly methane |
| **Biogas (gobar gas)** | mainly methane |
| **Bhopal gas tragedy (1984)** | methyl isocyanate (MIC) |
| **Carbon monoxide** | poisonous — binds haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin |
| **Gas in common fire extinguishers** | carbon dioxide |

### More common names of compounds

| Common name | Chemical name / formula |
|---|---|
| **Caustic soda** | sodium hydroxide (NaOH) |
| **Blue vitriol** | copper sulphate (CuSO₄·5H₂O) |
| **Green vitriol** | ferrous sulphate (FeSO₄·7H₂O) |
| **Gypsum** | calcium sulphate dihydrate (CaSO₄·2H₂O) |
| **Limestone, marble and chalk** | calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) |
| **Sand (quartz)** | silicon dioxide (SiO₂) |
| **Potash alum (phitkari)** | used to purify water (makes impurities settle) |
| **Caustic potash** | potassium hydroxide (KOH) |

## Don't confuse
- **Tamarind = tartaric; tomato = oxalic; curd = lactic; ant sting = formic.**
- **LPG = butane mainly; CNG and biogas = methane.**
- **Blue vitriol** = copper sulphate; **green vitriol** = ferrous sulphate; **oil of vitriol** = sulphuric acid.
- **Gypsum** (CaSO₄·2H₂O) is heated to make **Plaster of Paris** (CaSO₄·½H₂O).

**Remember it:** "Vinegar-Acetic, Lemon-Citric, Tamarind-Tartaric, Curd-Lactic, Ant-Formic."

**TL;DR**
- Stomach acid = hydrochloric acid; antacid = milk of magnesia (magnesium hydroxide).
- Aqua regia (HCl : HNO₃ = 3 : 1) dissolves gold.
- Laughing gas N₂O; dry ice solid CO₂; Bhopal 1984 = methyl isocyanate.
keyPoints: Vinegar — acetic (ethanoic) acid.
Lemon and orange — citric acid.
Litmus — natural indicator from lichens; acid turns blue litmus red, base turns red litmus blue.
Milk of magnesia — magnesium hydroxide — an antacid.
Laughing gas — nitrous oxide (N₂O).
Dry ice — solid carbon dioxide.
Limestone, marble and chalk — calcium carbonate (CaCO₃).
Potash alum (phitkari) — used to purify water (makes impurities settle).

items.title: Chemistry V — Ores, Alloys, Corrosion, Hard Water, Polymers & Reactions
items.body:
## Metals in use, water, plastics and reaction types

**In one line:** metals come from named ores, are blended into alloys and protected from rust; water hardness, soaps and polymers complete the everyday chemistry.

**Why it is asked:** "bauxite is an ore of?", "German silver contains?", "galvanisation is coating with?", "temporary hardness is removed by?" and "Teflon / Bakelite" are frequent single-fact items.

**The story**

Iron rusts only when **both oxygen (air) and water** are present; coating it with **zinc** (galvanisation) protects it. Hardness of water comes from calcium and magnesium salts: **bicarbonates** cause **temporary** hardness that boiling removes, while **chlorides and sulphates** cause **permanent** hardness. Soap forms scum in hard water, but synthetic detergents still lather. Plastics come in two families: **thermoplastics** (polythene, PVC) soften on heating and can be remoulded, while **thermosetting** plastics such as **Bakelite** set hard for ever.

### Ores of metals

| Ore | Metal |
|---|---|
| **Bauxite** | aluminium |
| **Haematite (and magnetite)** | iron |
| **Cinnabar** | mercury |
| **Galena** | lead |
| **Zinc blende** | zinc |
| **Chalcopyrite (copper pyrites)** | copper |

### More alloys

| Alloy | Composition / use |
|---|---|
| **Solder** | lead + tin (joining wires) |
| **German silver** | copper + zinc + nickel — contains no silver |
| **Amalgam** | mercury + another metal (dental fillings) |
| **Duralumin** | aluminium + copper (with magnesium, manganese) — aircraft bodies |
| **Gun metal** | copper + tin + zinc |
| **Bell metal** | copper + tin (more tin than bronze) |
| **Magnalium** | aluminium + magnesium |
| **22-carat gold** | 22 parts gold + 2 parts copper or silver (24 carat = pure gold) |

### Corrosion, storage and water

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Rusting of iron** | needs both oxygen (air) and water; rust is hydrated iron oxide |
| **Galvanisation** | coating iron or steel with zinc |
| **Green coating on copper** | basic copper carbonate |
| **Silver turns black** | silver sulphide forms |
| **Sodium and potassium are stored in** | kerosene (they react violently with air and water) |
| **White phosphorus is stored in** | water (it catches fire in air) |
| **Temporary hardness of water** | calcium and magnesium bicarbonates; removed by boiling |
| **Permanent hardness of water** | chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium; removed by washing soda or ion exchange |
| **Soap** | sodium or potassium salt of fatty acids; forms scum in hard water (detergents do not) |
| **Saponification** | making soap from fat or oil and sodium hydroxide |
| **Disinfecting drinking water** | chlorine or bleaching powder |

### Polymers and carbon compounds in use

| Material | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Teflon (PTFE)** | non-stick coating of cookware |
| **Nylon** | first fully synthetic fibre (Wallace Carothers, 1935) |
| **Bakelite** | thermosetting plastic — electrical switches and handles |
| **Thermoplastics (polythene, PVC)** | soften on heating and can be remoulded |
| **Rayon** | artificial silk made from cellulose (wood pulp) |
| **Natural rubber** | polymer of isoprene; hardened by vulcanisation with sulphur (Goodyear) |
| **PET (polyethylene terephthalate)** | bottles and polyester fibre |
| **Fullerene (C₆₀, "buckyball")** | football-shaped allotrope of carbon |
| **Methanol** | poisonous alcohol — can cause blindness and death (spurious liquor) |
| **Ethanol** | alcohol of drinks; made by fermentation of sugar by yeast |
| **Octane number** | measures anti-knocking quality of petrol (cetane number for diesel) |

### Chemical laws and reaction types

| Law / reaction | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Law of conservation of mass** | Antoine Lavoisier — mass is neither created nor destroyed in a reaction |
| **Law of definite (constant) proportions** | Joseph Proust — a compound always has elements in a fixed mass ratio |
| **Atomic theory (1808)** | John Dalton |
| **Exothermic reactions** | give out heat — burning of fuels and respiration |
| **Endothermic reactions** | absorb energy — photosynthesis, dissolving ammonium chloride |
| **Oxidation and reduction** | oxidation = gain of oxygen or loss of electrons; reduction is the reverse |
| **Catalyst** | changes the rate of a reaction without being used up; enzymes are biological catalysts |
| **Artificial ripening of fruit** | calcium carbide (releases acetylene) is banned; ethylene gas is the permitted ripener |

### Fertilisers

| Nutrient / fertiliser | Role or content |
|---|---|
| **Nitrogen (N)** | leafy green growth (protein and chlorophyll) |
| **Phosphorus (P)** | root development, flowering and seed formation |
| **Potassium (K)** | disease resistance and fruit quality |
| **Urea** | about 46% nitrogen — the richest common nitrogen fertiliser |
| **DAP** | diammonium phosphate — supplies nitrogen and phosphorus |

## Don't confuse
- **German silver has no silver** (copper + zinc + nickel); **solder** = lead + tin; **amalgam** always contains mercury.
- **Galvanisation = zinc coating**; tinning = tin coating.
- **Temporary** hardness (bicarbonates) goes on boiling; **permanent** hardness (chlorides, sulphates) does not.
- **Bakelite = thermosetting**; polythene and PVC = thermoplastics. **Methanol** is poisonous; **ethanol** is drinking alcohol.

**Remember it:** "Bauxite-Aluminium, Haematite-Iron, Cinnabar-Mercury, Galena-Lead."

**TL;DR**
- Rust needs air and water; zinc coating (galvanising) prevents it; sodium is kept in kerosene.
- Exothermic: burning, respiration; endothermic: photosynthesis.
- Lavoisier = conservation of mass; Dalton = atomic theory (1808); Proust = definite proportions.
- N = leaves, P = roots, K = disease resistance; urea about 46% nitrogen.
keyPoints: Bauxite — aluminium.
Haematite (and magnetite) — iron.
Solder — lead + tin (joining wires).
German silver — copper + zinc + nickel — contains no silver.
Rusting of iron — needs both oxygen (air) and water; rust is hydrated iron oxide.
Galvanisation — coating iron or steel with zinc.
Teflon (PTFE) — non-stick coating of cookware.
Nylon — first fully synthetic fibre (Wallace Carothers, 1935).
