items.title: Biology II — Cell Organelles, Cell Division, Heredity & Plant Physiology
items.body:
## Inside the cell, and how plants live

**In one line:** each organelle has one job, cell division makes body cells (mitosis) or sex cells (meiosis), and plants move water up the xylem and food through the phloem.

**Why it is asked:** "suicide bags of the cell", "protein factory", "cell theory was given by", "number of chromosomes in humans", "fruit-ripening hormone" and "Rhizobium" are high-frequency PSC items.

**The story**

**Robert Hooke (1665)** named "cells" after seeing dead cork; **Leeuwenhoek** first saw living cells. **Schleiden** (plants, 1838) and **Schwann** (animals, 1839) proposed that all living things are made of cells — the **cell theory** — and **Virchow** added that every cell comes from a pre-existing cell. Bacteria are **prokaryotes**: their DNA lies free, with no nuclear membrane. In plants, water and minerals climb the **xylem** while food made in leaves travels in the **phloem**; five hormone families control growth.

### Cell — discoveries and organelles

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Cell first described (cork, 1665)** | Robert Hooke |
| **First to see living cells (bacteria, protozoa)** | Antonie van Leeuwenhoek |
| **Cell theory (1838–39)** | Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann |
| **"Every cell arises from a pre-existing cell"** | Rudolf Virchow |
| **Ribosomes** | protein synthesis ("protein factories") |
| **Lysosomes** | "suicide bags" — digestive enzymes that break down waste |
| **Golgi apparatus** | packaging and secretion of materials |
| **Endoplasmic reticulum** | transport network; rough ER makes proteins, smooth ER makes lipids |
| **Centrosome (centrioles)** | found in animal cells; helps in cell division |
| **Mitochondria and chloroplasts** | have their own DNA and ribosomes |
| **Prokaryotic cells (bacteria)** | no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles |
| **Largest single cell** | egg of the ostrich |
| **Longest cell of the human body** | nerve cell (neuron) |
| **Smallest cell** | Mycoplasma (PPLO) |

### Cell division and heredity

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Mitosis** | division of body cells giving two identical daughter cells — growth and repair |
| **Meiosis** | division that forms gametes and halves the chromosome number |
| **Chromosomes in a human body cell** | 46 (23 pairs) |
| **Sex of a child** | decided by the father's sperm (X or Y chromosome); XX = girl, XY = boy |
| **Father of genetics** | Gregor Mendel — experiments on the garden pea |
| **Double-helix model of DNA (1953)** | James Watson and Francis Crick |

### Plant physiology and plant hormones

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Xylem** | carries water and minerals up from the roots |
| **Phloem** | carries food made in leaves to all parts (translocation) |
| **Stomata** | leaf pores for gas exchange and transpiration |
| **Oxygen released in photosynthesis** | comes from the splitting of water (photolysis) |
| **Auxin** | cell elongation; bending of shoots towards light (phototropism) |
| **Gibberellin** | stem elongation and bolting; breaks seed dormancy |
| **Cytokinin** | promotes cell division; delays ageing of leaves |
| **Abscisic acid** | "stress hormone" — closes stomata and keeps seeds dormant |
| **Ethylene** | gaseous hormone that ripens fruit |
| **Rhizobium** | bacterium in root nodules of legumes that fixes atmospheric nitrogen |
| **Pitcher plant (Nepenthes)** | insectivorous plant (traps insects for nitrogen) |
| **Cuscuta (dodder)** | parasitic plant without chlorophyll |

### Classification of living things

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Binomial nomenclature (genus + species)** | Carl Linnaeus — father of taxonomy |
| **Five-kingdom classification (1969)** | R.H. Whittaker |
| **Father of biology (and of zoology)** | Aristotle |
| **Father of botany** | Theophrastus |
| **Scientific name of humans** | Homo sapiens |

## Don't confuse
- **Lysosome = suicide bag; ribosome = protein factory; Golgi = packaging; mitochondria = powerhouse.**
- **Mitosis** keeps the chromosome number (growth); **meiosis** halves it (gametes).
- **Xylem = water up; phloem = food around.**
- **Ethylene ripens fruit; abscisic acid closes stomata; auxin bends shoots to light.**

**Remember it:** "Hooke saw cork, Schleiden–Schwann wrote cell theory, Mendel bred peas."

**TL;DR**
- Humans have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs); the father's X or Y decides the child's sex.
- Rhizobium fixes nitrogen in legume root nodules.
- Linnaeus = binomial nomenclature; Whittaker = five kingdoms (1969).
keyPoints: Cell first described (cork, 1665) — Robert Hooke.
Cell theory (1838–39) — Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann.
Mitosis — division of body cells giving two identical daughter cells — growth and repair.
Meiosis — division that forms gametes and halves the chromosome number.
Xylem — carries water and minerals up from the roots.
Phloem — carries food made in leaves to all parts (translocation).
Binomial nomenclature (genus + species) — Carl Linnaeus — father of taxonomy.
items.source: NCERT Science Class 6–10 and Class 11–12 Physics/Chemistry/Biology (standard treatment); BIPM SI brochure; PYQ bank .research/pyq-bank/sci-general-science-basics.md

items.title: Biology III — Human Body: Numbers, Blood, Digestion, Brain, Glands & Vitamins
items.body:
## The human body by numbers and functions

**In one line:** a few dozen body facts — bone counts, blood cells, enzymes, brain parts, glands and vitamins — make up most human-biology questions.

**Why it is asked:** "smallest bone", "largest organ", "normal blood pressure", "blood groups discovered by", "bile is secreted by", "balance is controlled by" and "vitamin made by sunlight" recur across APPSC, UPSC and SSC papers.

**The story**

An adult has **206 bones**; the **femur** (thigh) is the longest and the **stapes** in the middle ear the smallest. Blood carries oxygen in **red blood cells**, whose iron-rich **haemoglobin** binds oxygen; they live about **120 days** and are made in the **bone marrow**. **Karl Landsteiner** discovered the ABO blood groups in **1900**. Food digestion starts in the mouth with salivary amylase and finishes in the small intestine, helped by **bile** from the liver (stored in the gall bladder), which breaks fat into tiny droplets. The **cerebrum** thinks and remembers, while the **cerebellum** keeps balance.

### Body records and numbers

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Bones in an adult human** | 206 (a newborn has about 300) |
| **Longest bone** | femur (thigh bone) |
| **Smallest bone** | stapes (stirrup) in the middle ear |
| **Largest organ of the body** | skin |
| **Teeth in an adult** | 32 |
| **Hardest substance in the body** | tooth enamel |
| **Normal blood pressure** | 120/80 mm of mercury (systolic/diastolic) |
| **Human heart** | four chambers; beats about 72 times a minute at rest |
| **Circulation of blood discovered by** | William Harvey (1628) |
| **Blood volume of an adult** | about 5–6 litres |

### Blood

| Component / discovery | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Red blood cells** | carry oxygen using iron-rich haemoglobin; live about 120 days; made in bone marrow |
| **White blood cells** | fight infection (immunity) |
| **Platelets** | help blood to clot |
| **Spleen** | "graveyard of RBCs" — destroys old red cells |
| **ABO blood groups (1900)** | Karl Landsteiner |
| **Rh factor (1940)** | Landsteiner and Wiener — named after the rhesus monkey |
| **Plasma** | liquid part of blood, about 55% of its volume |

### Digestion and respiration

| Organ / enzyme | Role |
|---|---|
| **Salivary amylase (ptyalin)** | begins digestion of starch in the mouth |
| **Pepsin (with hydrochloric acid)** | digests proteins in the stomach |
| **Bile** | made by the liver, stored in the gall bladder; emulsifies fats (contains no enzyme) |
| **Pancreatic juice** | trypsin (proteins), lipase (fats) and amylase (starch) |
| **Villi of the small intestine** | absorb digested food (most absorption happens here) |
| **Large intestine** | absorbs water from undigested food |
| **Muscle cramps after hard exercise** | lactic acid from anaerobic respiration |

### Brain and endocrine glands

| Part / gland | Function or hormone |
|---|---|
| **Cerebrum** | largest part of the brain — intelligence, memory, thinking, voluntary actions |
| **Cerebellum** | balance and posture; coordination of movement |
| **Hypothalamus** | controls body temperature, hunger and thirst |
| **Reflex actions** | controlled by the spinal cord |
| **Islets of Langerhans (pancreas)** | insulin (lowers blood sugar) and glucagon (raises it) |
| **Diabetes mellitus** | too little insulin (or the body not responding to it) |
| **Growth hormone (pituitary)** | excess in childhood causes gigantism; deficiency causes dwarfism |
| **Parathyroid gland** | parathormone controls calcium level in blood |
| **Pineal gland** | melatonin — sleep–wake cycle |
| **Thymus** | maturation of T-lymphocytes (immunity); shrinks in adults |

### Vitamins and nutrition — beyond the basic list

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Fat-soluble vitamins** | A, D, E and K (B and C are water-soluble) |
| **Vitamin D** | made in the skin on exposure to sunlight; deficiency causes rickets |
| **Vitamin K** | needed for clotting of blood |
| **Vitamin E** | antioxidant; needed for fertility |
| **Vitamin B12** | contains cobalt; deficiency causes pernicious anaemia |
| **Vitamin B3 (niacin)** | deficiency causes pellagra |
| **Chemical names of vitamins** | A = retinol, B1 = thiamine, C = ascorbic acid, D = calciferol |
| **Vitamin C and cooking** | vitamin C is destroyed easily by heat |
| **Kwashiorkor** | protein deficiency in children (swollen belly) |
| **Marasmus** | deficiency of both protein and calories (wasting) |

## Don't confuse
- **Femur** is the longest bone; **stapes** the smallest; **skin** the largest organ; **liver** the largest gland.
- **Bile** has no enzyme — it only emulsifies fat; it is **made by the liver** and **stored in the gall bladder**.
- **Cerebrum** = thinking and memory; **cerebellum** = balance; **medulla** = heartbeat and breathing.
- **Kwashiorkor** = protein only; **marasmus** = protein and calories.

**Remember it:** "Fat-soluble vitamins are DEKA (D, E, K, A)."

**TL;DR**
- 206 bones; normal BP 120/80 mm Hg; RBCs live about 120 days.
- Landsteiner discovered ABO groups (1900); Harvey discovered circulation.
- Vitamin D from sunlight; K for clotting; B12 has cobalt (pernicious anaemia).
keyPoints: Bones in an adult human — 206 (a newborn has about 300).
Longest bone — femur (thigh bone).
Red blood cells — carry oxygen using iron-rich haemoglobin; live about 120 days; made in bone marrow.
Platelets — help blood to clot.
Salivary amylase (ptyalin) — begins digestion of starch in the mouth.
Pepsin (with hydrochloric acid) — digests proteins in the stomach.
Cerebrum — largest part of the brain — intelligence, memory, thinking, voluntary actions.
Cerebellum — balance and posture; coordination of movement.

items.title: For Mains — Science in daily life & scientific temper
items.body:
**In one line**
For Mains (Paper-5, clause M5-1 'S&T in daily life'), basic science is not recalled as facts but used to argue how scientific literacy improves health, safety, agriculture and governance.

**The analytical frame**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Significance | science literacy → safer homes, better health choices, higher farm yields, informed citizens |
| Everyday physics | electrical safety (fuse in series, earthing), optics (spectacles, mirrors), pressure cooker, solar cooker |
| Everyday chemistry | pH and acids/bases in cleaning and antacids, lime for water/soil, food-adulteration awareness |
| Everyday biology | balanced diet, vitamin-deficiency diseases, immunisation, hygiene lower the disease burden |
| Governance link | uptake of immunisation, salt iodisation, ORS, food fortification; countering misinformation and superstition |
| Criticism / limits | low science spend (~0.65% of GDP), rural awareness gaps, pseudoscience, poor last-mile communication |
| Way forward | school science reform, public-communication campaigns, Article 51A(h) scientific temper as a civic goal |

**Data, provisions and examples to quote**
- **Article 51A(h)** — developing scientific temper is a Fundamental Duty.
- India's R&D spend ≈ **0.65% of GDP** (target ~2%), below major economies — a standing criticism.
